items: A royalty is a claim on revenue, not on profit — and not equity. The investor pays upfront for a contractual right to a fixed percentage of an asset’s revenue; opex, capex and cost inflation stay with the operator. The result is exposure to price and volume with none of the margin risk — which is why royalties have historically hedged inflation.

A ~USD 2tn market, institutionalizing fast. Established sectors: pharma ~USD 185bn, green metals ~USD 260bn, US natural gas ~USD 140bn, music ~USD 70bn; emerging: brands, carbon offsets, sports. Fund product has moved from closed-end specialists to evergreen platforms.

Between private credit and private equity — until bankruptcy. Typical market gross returns of 10-14%, vs 8-12% for private credit and 18-22% for buyouts; cash-yielding from day one, upside geared to the asset, downside structurable like credit. In insolvency, however, position depends entirely on legal form: a property interest survives the operator; a contractual claim ranks unsecured.

Self-liquidating cash flows make exit optional — and evergreen natural. Royalties can be underwritten on a hold-for-life basis; the four exit routes (run-off, secondary sale, operator buy-back, securitization/portfolio sale) are upside, not requirement. The same feature supplies the internal liquidity, J-curve-free entry and data-anchored NAVs that semi-liquid structures need.

Risk lives in three places, none of them a payment waterfall: revenue sustainability (volume/price), operator going-concern, and contract legal strength. Sector-specific expressions: streaming royalty rates and catalog decay (music), patent cliffs (pharma), commodity price (gas).

The investable universe is a 2×2 of sector focus × structure. PG Diversified Royalties (multi-sector evergreen; 8.9% annualized net since Q4 2020), HCRx (pharma evergreen; 12.6% net in 2025), Primary Wave and HarbourView (music closed-end). Liquidity mechanics — monthly NAV vs a four-yearly run-off option vs GP-led secondary sales — differ more than the headline labels suggest.

blocks.text: What is a Royalty
A contractual claim on revenue, senior to every cost line

blocks.html: In its simplest form, a royalty investor pays an upfront amount to the owner or operator of a revenue-generating asset in exchange for the contractual right to receive a percentage of that asset’s revenue. Qualifying assets are rights to intellectual property — drug patents, music copyrights, brand trademarks — and exclusive rights over natural resources such as gas or minerals. Payments are scheduled monthly or quarterly, the payor is required to deliver regular sales reports, and contracts typically carry periodic audit rights. An investor can either buy a royalty that already exists, or create one — a "synthetic royalty" — by providing capital to an operator in exchange for a share of the revenue the asset generates.
blocks.text: In its simplest form, a royalty investor pays an upfront amount to the owner or operator of a revenue-generating asset in exchange for the contractual right to receive a percentage of that asset’s revenue. Qualifying assets are rights to intellectual property — drug patents, music copyrights, brand trademarks — and exclusive rights over natural resources such as gas or minerals. Payments are scheduled monthly or quarterly, the payor is required to deliver regular sales reports, and contracts typically carry periodic audit rights. An investor can either buy a royalty that already exists, or create one — a "synthetic royalty" — by providing capital to an operator in exchange for a share of the revenue the asset generates.

blocks.html: The defining feature is where the claim sits. The royalty is carved out of revenue before any cost line: the investor is not responsible for funding opex or capex and is therefore insensitive to cost inflation and profit margins. Exposure is to revenue drivers — price and volume — only. This is also the inflation-hedge mechanism: payments rise with price while cost inflation is absorbed entirely by the operator. Exhibit 1 makes the point with numbers: in the inflation scenario, revenue +20% lifts the royalty by exactly 20%, while the operator’s profit is flat because costs rose faster.

blocks.text: Between private credit and private equity — until bankruptcy

blocks.html: The structured nature of royalty contracts gives clarity and control over payment terms and durations, akin to private credit; unlike credit, royalties also carry upside geared to the underlying asset’s performance. This places the risk-return profile between private credit and private equity. Royalties are cash-yielding from day one, which builds MOIC through the holding period; where the IP is long-lived (music) or the right is a sub-surface ownership, yield is complemented by potential long-term NAV accretion.

blocks.html: The comparison above describes normal operation. In stress, position depends on something the marketing materials rarely dwell on: legal form. Where the royalty constitutes a property interest attached to the asset — US mineral rights are real property ownership of the sub-surface — the claim travels with the asset through an operator insolvency or change of control. Where the royalty is only a contractual claim against the operator (the case for many pharma and media royalties), the investor ranks as an unsecured creditor and the contract can be compromised in a restructuring. Two instruments with identical economics in good times can therefore sit at opposite ends of the capital structure in bad times. The instrument mix is DD question ② in the fund section.

blocks.text: Sector Deep Dives
Music: the most institutionalized royalty market

blocks.html: Music gets the longest treatment here not because it is the largest market — on PG’s own sizing it is the smallest of the four established sectors — but because it is the most institutionalized: rights are fully assignable, income data arrives monthly, the specialist GP population is the deepest, and it is where allocator deal flow actually shows up. Every song carries two separate copyrights: the masters (the specific recording, controlled by artists and record labels) and the composition (notes, melodies, lyrics — controlled by songwriters and publishers). blocks.html: Follow the dollar through a stream. Of a USD 10 consumer payment to a streaming platform, the platform retains ~USD 3.5; ~USD 5.2 flows to the recording side, of which the label keeps ~USD 3.9 and the artist receives ~USD 1.3; and ~USD 1.3 flows to the publishing side, split roughly evenly between publisher and songwriter at ~USD 0.65 each. Administrators — labels, publishers and performance rights organizations — collect, take their contractual cut, and pass the remainder to the rightsholder: the Net Publisher’s Share (NPS), which is the cash flow a royalty investor actually buys and the unit in which catalogs are priced. A portion of US publishing income is set by statutory rates rather than free negotiation — a regulatory lever that sits directly on the revenue line.

blocks.html: Market. blocks.html: Duration and valuation. US copyright runs for the life of the (last surviving) artist plus 70 years (minimum 50 years by jurisdiction) — the perpetual-growing family of Exhibit 9. Catalogs trade at multiples of NPS; transaction multiples for publishing catalogs have risen over the last decade, and HVEP sizes its pipeline using a standardized 15x multiple on annual revenue — a useful rough anchor for where the market clears, and a sensitivity every music-fund underwriting should run both ways.

blocks.html: Underwriting. Catalog acquisitions are underwritten by forecasting royalties with decay curves — observed consumption patterns by genre and income type — overlaid with market growth. Mature catalogs are predictable; the idiosyncratic risk is the artist: conduct issues can see songs temporarily pulled from streaming platforms. PG’s stated discipline — seasoned catalogs only, zero value to unreleased music, artists in good standing — is the passive end of the strategy spectrum. The active end is Primary Wave, whose model is to buy iconic catalogs and market them to lift NPS: catalogs held in Fund 1 had achieved 92% cumulative NPS growth since purchase as of 2024 (Fund 2: 76%; Fund 3: 41%). HarbourView sits on a data/sourcing axis: ~28,100 songs accumulated since 2021 and a proprietary ingestion platform ("HITS") driving underwriting. The strategy choice matters for DD because it determines what the return actually is: beta to streaming growth, or alpha from marketing execution that must be re-proven catalog by catalog.

blocks.text: Pharmaceuticals: the original royalty market

blocks.html: How the royalties come to exist. Drug IP typically originates with inventors who cannot manufacture or distribute at scale — academic institutions and small biopharma — and is licensed to large pharma in exchange for royalty payments on future sales. Those royalty entitlements are then monetized: IP holders sell them to investors, usually to fund further R&D ("traditional royalty"); alternatively an investor pays a pharma company upfront for a share of a product’s future sales ("synthetic royalty"). Large pharma’s patent cliffs keep the machine running — big companies replace expiring revenue by buying external innovation, transferring IP from emerging biopharma and creating royalties in the process; the emerging companies are voracious consumers of capital and increasingly sell royalties to fund growth.

blocks.html: The supply side is structural. Emerging biopharma now originates ~72% of new regulatory filings, up from 65% in 2014. The sector consumed over USD 310bn of funding across 2020-24; the average R&D investment to progress a drug from discovery to launch has reached ~USD 2.3bn; and the capital required to sustain biopharma innovation over the next decade is projected to exceed USD 1tn. Among the three channels in the biopharma capital stack, royalties are the only one that is simultaneously non-dilutive, operationally light and product-specific (Exhibit 27) — which is why monetization volumes keep compounding.

US natural gas: royalties as real property

blocks.html: Mineral rights are the real-property ownership of everything beneath the surface, and private ownership of them exists essentially only in the US (and a small part of Canada) — elsewhere sub-surface rights belong to governments. The investor acquires the mineral rights and leases them to operators, receiving an upfront lease bonus plus a royalty of 12.5-25% of gross production revenue, with no liability for any capital or operating costs. The instrument hierarchy — fee minerals (perpetual, strongest) > ORRI (lease-linked) > NPI (cost-burdened) — is Exhibit 6’s legal-strength spectrum in its purest form: fee minerals are the one corner of the royalty universe where the claim is unambiguously senior to the operator’s entire capital structure, because it is not a claim on the operator at all.

blocks.html: Market and thesis. PG frames US natural gas royalties as a ~USD 140bn addressable market (as of Dec-23), 12-15% gross return targets, long-term duration. The demand thesis: natural gas’s share of US energy consumption rose from 18% in 2005 to 39% in 2023; ~25% of global energy demand growth through 2040 is projected to be met by gas; over 200 US coal plants are expected to be decommissioned or converted to gas; and the US is now the world’s largest producer, with AI / data-center load growth and rising LNG exports as incremental drivers. The offsetting exposure is the commodity itself: the royalty hedges cost inflation, not the gas price. Volume × spot is the revenue line, and the price leg is the piece prudent investors hedge.

blocks.text: Emerging sectors: large numbers, thin markets

blocks.html: Green metals (~USD 260bn) is established on PG’s map — royalty interests over mines producing the metals behind renewable technologies — while brands (~USD 320bn), carbon offsets (~USD 186bn, MSCI Trove-based) and sports (~USD 36bn, Deloitte / PwC-based) are the emerging tail. The pattern to expect: first movers earn pricing power against limited competition, but secondary depth is shallow, valuation marks are soft, and exit depends on the asset class continuing to institutionalize. In fund DD these sleeves deserve the concentration treatment, not the diversification credit.

blocks.html: Sports: institutionalization first, royalties next. The preconditions that made music and pharma royalty-investable are now assembling in sports. The revenue pool is contracting and compounding: the global sports market is projected to grow 44% from 2025 to USD 602bn by 2030, and media rights — the most contract-like revenue line in the ecosystem — grew 41% from USD 41bn in 2020 to USD 58bn in 2025, heading for ~USD 67bn by end-2026, with streaming platforms now controlling roughly 20% of the market. Governance frameworks for institutional capital are in place: private equity deal count in sports is up 284% since 2018, every major US league now admits institutional investors — the NFL, the largest league at over USD 23bn of 2024 revenue, was the last to open in 2024 — and average franchise valuations have compounded at 14% a year since 2020. Contracted, growing revenue pools plus league-sanctioned capital frameworks are precisely the substrate that royalty-like claims are written on.
blocks.text: Sports: institutionalization first, royalties next. The preconditions that made music and pharma royalty-investable are now assembling in sports. The revenue pool is contracting and compounding: the global sports market is projected to grow 44% from 2025 to USD 602bn by 2030, and media rights — the most contract-like revenue line in the ecosystem — grew 41% from USD 41bn in 2020 to USD 58bn in 2025, heading for ~USD 67bn by end-2026, with streaming platforms now controlling roughly 20% of the market. Governance frameworks for institutional capital are in place: private equity deal count in sports is up 284% since 2018, every major US league now admits institutional investors — the NFL, the largest league at over USD 23bn of 2024 revenue, was the last to open in 2024 — and average franchise valuations have compounded at 14% a year since 2020. Contracted, growing revenue pools plus league-sanctioned capital frameworks are precisely the substrate that royalty-like claims are written on.

blocks.note: Note: Franchise-valuation CAGR per the same source. Source: Goldman Sachs; Junson redraw.

blocks.html: Where royalty structures are already forming: collegiate sport. The 2021 NCAA v. Alston ruling ended amateur-status protections; donor collectives began paying athletes for their name, image and likeness — NIL is a licensing royalty in all but name — and the 2025 NCAA settlement added USD 2.8bn of back damages plus a framework for schools to share revenue with athletes directly. The money is real: Division 1 FBS football generated USD 7bn of revenue in FY2024-25, with the Big Ten and SEC each above USD 1bn. To fund the new landscape, universities are standing up for-profit commercial entities that raise private capital against athletic-department revenues — Otro Capital’s USD 500mm into Utah’s Crimson Brand Partners, RedBird’s investment into the Big 12 alongside a USD 30mm credit line to member schools — structures one documentation cycle away from the synthetic royalties of Section 1. The distinction to hold onto: franchise equity earns valuation multiples, a royalty earns a revenue share — the sports bull case in circulation belongs to the former, and the ~USD 36bn sizing in Exhibit 8 remains the addressable figure for the latter. The gap between the two is the opportunity to watch.

blocks.text: Exit and Fund Structure
Four exit routes — all of them optional

blocks.html: Because a royalty amortizes itself, "exit" is not the load-bearing part of the return. Royalties are largely self-liquidating — not reliant on an exit to meet target returns — and sale is an upside case, not the plan. Four routes exist, with very different depth by sector:

rows: Collect the contracted cash flows to depletion / expiry; underwrite hold-for-life
The default. Requires no market at all

blocks.text: Why the asset class migrated to evergreen

blocks.html: PG’s stated case for evergreen royalty funds is alignment: the structures match the longer-term nature of the assets and pair them with liquidity provisions. The underlying logic is that royalties neutralize, one by one, the classic failure points of semi-liquid structures:
blocks.text: PG’s stated case for evergreen royalty funds is alignment: the structures match the longer-term nature of the assets and pair them with liquidity provisions. The underlying logic is that royalties neutralize, one by one, the classic failure points of semi-liquid structures:

items: ① Internal liquidity. Redemptions can be met from contractual cash flow rather than forced asset sales. The scale is material: HCRx’s evergreen portfolio generated ~USD 228mm of 2025 free cash flow on a USD 2bn+ portfolio fair value — roughly 11% of portfolio value returning as cash in a year.

② No J-curve, no vintage lottery. Returns are yield-led and begin on day one, so any entry point buys a producing portfolio — HCRx markets exactly this: immediate ownership of 50+ approved products across 40+ therapeutic areas, with capital compounding far sooner than in a drawdown fund. The drawdown alternative forces deployment deadlines and concentrates each fund in a single pricing vintage.

③ NAV with data anchors. Royalty NAVs discount observable, high-frequency revenue data — prescription scripts, streaming statements, production reports — rather than comparable-company multiples. Still GP-marked (see DD question ⑤), but the inputs are harder to argue with than most private-asset marks.

blocks.text: Downside Risk and DD Framework
Risk lives in three places — none of them a payment waterfall

blocks.html: In normal operation the royalty is paid first, so the credit-style question "who ranks ahead of me" is the wrong frame. The three dimensions that actually determine loss are: whether the revenue persists, whether the operator keeps producing it, and what the contract is worth when the operator fails. PG’s own risk list — sector regulatory change, technology shifts, consumer behavior, counterparty risk, legal and regulatory risk, concentration, asset impairment and operational issues at the operating company — sorts cleanly into these three:
blocks.text: In normal operation the royalty is paid first, so the credit-style question "who ranks ahead of me" is the wrong frame. The three dimensions that actually determine loss are: whether the revenue persists, whether the operator keeps producing it, and what the contract is worth when the operator fails. PG’s own risk list — sector regulatory change, technology shifts, consumer behavior, counterparty risk, legal and regulatory risk, concentration, asset impairment and operational issues at the operating company — sorts cleanly into these three:

rows: Volume decays faster than underwritten; price falls or is re-set

Music: decay-curve deviation; statutory / streaming royalty rates; artist conduct pulling songs from platforms. Pharma: patent cliff timing, superior entrants, pricing & reimbursement. Gas / metals: spot price
Seasoned assets; genre- and income-type decay curves; no value to unreleased music; post-approval products only; price hedging
Production stops — royalty on zero revenue is zero, regardless of seniority
Single-operator exposure in gas; marketer concentration in pharma; label / DSP disputes in music
Operator diversification; audit rights and sales reporting; established marketers (HCRx: approved products sold by established pharma)
Contractual claim compromised in restructuring; license rejected
Pharma / media royalties as unsecured contract claims vs fee minerals as real property
"Prudent structuring and documentation are essential"; prefer property-interest instruments; step-up / step-down economics and make-whole payments once hurdles hit

Five evaluation questions

items: ① What is the portfolio actually made of? Instrument mix — GRR / fee minerals / ORRI / NPI / stream / synthetic / RBN (Exhibit 6). The names are interchangeable in marketing; the cost exposure and insolvency treatment are not. An "NPI-heavy" gas book or an RBN-heavy media book is a different asset class from its label.

② What is the legal-strength mix? Share of NAV in property-interest form (registered mineral / mining interests) vs contractual claims against operators, cut by jurisdiction. This is the loss-given-stress driver the asset-level marketing skips.

③ What is the duration mix by revenue driver? Weight the book across Exhibit 9’s three families. A declining-annuity book (pharma) is self-liquidating; a perpetual-family book (music, fee minerals) parks its value in the terminal — fine, but only in a structure built to hold it.

④ Does the structure match the book? Cash-yield share of value vs the vehicle’s redemption terms; stress internal cash flow coverage of a redemption run. Note where each fund already sits on Exhibit 34’s spectrum — and that fee bases differ (HCRx charges on royalty receipts, not NAV), which changes the GP’s incentive between collecting cash and marking value.

⑤ Who marks the book, against what data? Valuer independence, third-party appraisal coverage, input data frequency (scripts / streaming statements / production reports), discount-rate policy vs rates, and realized-vs-NAV evidence. Track records built on hypothetical-liquidation NAVs deserve a different weight from realized DPI.

blocks.text: Type-specific watch items

items: PG: the "Diversified" label vs the book — Media is 46% of the portfolio and South Park alone 17.0% of NAV; single-name concentration of that size inside a monthly-NAV evergreen puts real weight on the mark. Also note the growth-stage pattern: H1-26 net 3.2% vs ~7% at asset level because 2026 vintage (36% of book) is held at cost — returns are being shaped by fundraising pace, in both directions.

HCRx: the liquidity term is the closest to closed-end of any evergreen in the set — a run-off option once every four years, with subscriptions queued. Treat it as a long-lock vehicle with evergreen accounting, not as semi-liquid. The receipts-based fee (~93bps of NAV historically) is cheap for the asset class but scales with collections, so model it against the book’s amortization profile.

Primary Wave: the headline IRRs are hypothetical-liquidation NAV figures; the only realized prints are GP-led sales to the affiliated Brookfield PCV — a related-party buyer, albeit at third-party-appraised prices. DD should test price discovery in those transactions and the independence of the appraisals; the Oct-23 DDQ is the starting point. The active-marketing alpha (NPS growth) is real but execution-dependent and must be re-proven each fund.

HarbourView: single-strategy exposure to music multiples: pipeline is sized at a standardized 15x, so underwrite the MOIC target against multiple compression as well as decay-curve risk; and as a 2021-founded firm, the track record predating Fund I is short.
